name: Mouseflow
tagline: Capture a small consented session sample and render a simple playback for debugging

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 500 sessions/month, 1 website project, 1 funnel, 1 month data retention, and unlimited users
tiers.notes: The first 14 days temporarily raise the allowance to 2,000 sessions, 5 website projects, and 10 funnels; afterward the permanent free caps apply.

tiers.name: Essential
tiers.limits: 5,000 sessions/month, 1 website project, 1 funnel, 3 months data retention, and unlimited users
tiers.notes: The live page displays $25/month in its fetched pricing state and advertises annual savings up to 35%, but the exact annual checkout amount was not exposed in accessible page text.

tiers.name: Advanced
tiers.limits: 25,000 sessions/month, 2 website projects, 5 funnels, 6 months data retention, and unlimited users
tiers.notes: The live page displays $109/month in its fetched pricing state; exact annual checkout amount not exposed in accessible page text.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: 100,000 sessions/month, 5 website projects, 10 funnels, 12 months data retention, and unlimited users
tiers.notes: The live page displays $319/month in its fetched pricing state; exact annual checkout amount not exposed in accessible page text.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom sessions, websites, funnels, retention, and support

pricing.freeTierCaps: 500 sessions/month, 1 website project, 1 funnel, 1 month data retention, and unlimited users
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (advertised savings up to 35%); 14-day no-card trial; 14-day money-back guarantee applies only to first-time annual non-Enterprise subscriptions
pricing.hiddenCosts: Tracking stops when the monthly session allowance runs out unless you manually buy/request a refill or upgrade; extended REST API access, SLA, and professional services are add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Mouseflow, capture a small consented session sample and render a simple playback for debugging. The hard boundary is capture compression, privacy redaction, storage, heatmaps, funnels, and hosted scale, plus data pipeline reliability and analytical depth.
coreLoopDIY: Capture a small consented sample of first-party session events, render a simple playback for debugging, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: capture compression, privacy redaction, storage, heatmaps, funnels, and hosted scale
moatNotes: data pipeline reliability and analytical depth
ongoingBurden: event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Mouseflow because teams pay because analytics must keep collecting and remain trustworthy while the product changes underneath it. The recurring cost buys event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Umami
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source privacy-focused web analytics platform.

alternatives.name: Microsoft Clarity
alternatives.desc: Unlimited session playback and heatmaps for free; the product is exactly as suspiciously generous as it sounds.

facts.install: Create a Clarity project and add its site-wide script directly or through a tag manager
facts.engines: Microsoft Copilot features are built in, but Clarity's public documentation does not identify the underlying foundation model
facts.dataFormat: Session recordings, heatmaps and events are stored in Microsoft's cloud; ordinary recordings are retained for a limited period, with selected favorites retained longer
facts.gapVsPaid: It lacks Mouseflow's deeper form analytics, feedback surveys, conversion funnels and dedicated commercial support, while data lives in Microsoft's cloud.
facts.setupBlocker: Insert the tracking script and complete the consent, privacy-disclosure and data-governance review appropriate to the site

alternatives.name: OpenReplay
alternatives.desc: Replay a consented sample with full debugging context, provided you are willing to run the stack.

facts.install: Create a hosted account or deploy to a public Ubuntu 24.04 server with the CLI or Helm; Docker Compose is experimental
facts.engines: The cloud product has AI summaries and natural-language querying, but its documentation does not identify the base model and the self-hosted edition does not include the cloud AI suite
facts.dataFormat: Replay and telemetry data live in the deployment's databases and object storage, or in OpenReplay's managed cloud when using the hosted service
facts.gapVsPaid: It is developer-debugging-first, harder to operate and weaker for turnkey form analytics, feedback and UX-research workflows.
facts.setupBlocker: Free self-hosting needs a public x86 Ubuntu server, domain and TLS, with at least about 2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM and 50 GB storage

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.desc: Replay, heatmaps and filters on a free allowance that is large enough for a small product.

facts.install: Create a PostHog Cloud project or use the hobby self-host script on a Linux server
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack splits analytics, transactions, queues and recordings across ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis and object storage; cloud data lives in PostHog's managed regions
facts.gapVsPaid: Session replay is one module inside a much larger product, with less dedicated form analytics, surveys and UX-research polish than Mouseflow.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting is an unsupported, resource-heavy multi-service stack requiring serious operations work

alternatives.name: Rybbit
alternatives.desc: Cookieless analytics and replay in one Compose file, with fewer forensic bells.

facts.install: Use the hosted service or deploy the free self-hosted edition with Docker Compose
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack uses PostgreSQL for application data, ClickHouse for analytics and Redis for queues and cache; hosted data lives in Rybbit's cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: Its replay and heatmap tooling is newer and less mature for form debugging, consent workflows and dedicated UX research than Mouseflow.
facts.setupBlocker: The indefinitely free path is self-hosting, which requires Docker Compose, a domain, secrets and enough resources for three data services

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a single-product first-party analytics DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Mouseflow in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: capture a small consented sample of first-party session events, render a simple playback for debugging, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Ship a lightweight browser SDK for page views and explicit custom events.
Create projects, API keys, environments, event names, and a documented event schema.
Ingest idempotently, filter obvious bots, truncate IP data, and avoid fingerprinting.
Build dashboards for visitors, sessions, funnels, retention, sources, pages, and events.
Expose filters by date, environment, device, country, referrer, and selected properties.
Add retention controls, raw-event export, deletion, health checks, and backup instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out cross-site identity graphs.
Deliberately leave out session replay and automatic DOM capture.
Deliberately leave out warehouse-scale reverse ETL and enterprise governance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
